I am going through a divorce, and ripping Tyranids apart as Assault is cathartic. This game is getting me through it.

Alright - to start off with I have to say I have been a huge 40k fan for decades, so normally any new title I buy regardless.

That having been said, 30 hours in, I will not be recommending this game to others - and I may get a significant amount of players trying to point bolters at my head for saying so, and I may well continue to play it more after I write this review.

Ok, so why the bad review?

Let's start with the good:  Lore, customisation, WH40K "feel", graphics.

The bad? Pretty much everything else, given what you are asked to spend on this title.

There is a campaign (which, since you can't advance your character class, or even pick one), whilst doing is an ok story but otherwise redundant.

There is PvE - PvE is probably the best part of the offering - 3 man coop...but its vs 7 maps and just repeatedly the same tactics, few moves, zergfest of aliens, interspersed with an occasional warping chaos marine platoon or two.  To say it is repetitive is calling it mildly; the first time you play its an adrenaline pump, the 2nd time you play a map it becomes a yawnfest and frankly, at any difficulty, goes down from there, as your weapons and skills just offset the difficulty rating.

PvP - I tried (a bit) and was just not good for me.  Your mileage may vary, but it seemed like this game was back in the 90s - yes campaign, yes coop, yes pvp (all modes which I think should still be mandatory in a title at this price), but this game was clearly a PvE bias with the additional modes tacked on.  There are much better PvE coops recently that do this much better, albeit without the 40k hit.

What really broke it for me, is that after 30 hours of playing repetitive maps with nothing but "difficulty scaling" (read bigger mob hp pools) offset by nothing but guns with bigger hits, is that I asked myself the question - if this was not 40k, would I have already stopped playing it?

Answer: Yes I would have.

TLDNR:  An better than average 40k offering in what has continued to be a mediocre universe of games medium.  If it wasn't 40k I would have refunded it as the only thing carrying it is that is 40k.

Space Marine 2, to me, is the best game I've played this year. From an astounding overworld and power-fantasy representation, to a refreshing new combat loop that enhances what the first Spacemarine title did to elevate the franchise from a TPS horde shooter to something more special. 

In this review I'll list the aspects of the game I feel are positive and negative regarding every game mode, and will be comparing SM 2 to SM 1 if needed in order to more easily introduce concepts. Also, I'll not be going into depth regarding the 6 playable classes, but might mention them if needed. 

[b]This review contains very minor spoilers relating to PVE and the Campaign.[/b]

[h2]General Points[/h2]

SM2 is a third person shooter with hack and slash as well as precision gameplay elements in which you are given access to three modes, a campaign that follows up on the first game, a pve mode that uses linear missions with random elements at every section to keep everything fresh (in which you can play 6 different classes that are upgradable and buildable), and a pvp mode  in which the same classes as in the pve can be played in a 6v6 manner in 3 different gamemodes.

[h3]New Mechanics: Precision-based gameplay[/h3]

SM 2 introduces a new mechanic the player can use to avoid melee damage, the parry. Similar to games like Sekiro and En Garde!, attacks from enemies in SM 2 can be parried in order to open up enemies to bursts of damage, giving more depth to a simple horde shooter formula like we had in the first game. 

Moreover, the classic dodge mechanic has also been included into the precision elements, making it so dodging certain attacks at the last moment also gives the player the option to highly damage enemies, and also being the only answer to certain unparriable attacks. 

The use of both these mechanics gives the game a refreshing learning curve that was almost non-existent in the first game, and gives some much needed depth when it comes to making combat more interesting against non-horde or special enemies.  

[h2]Campaing[/h2]

SM2's campaing is a good follow up to the first game's campaing, continuing Titus' story, but upping the spectacle and giving the characters more depth as well as presenting a world that feels more alive. Together with introducing massive waves of enemies as well as some decent boss encounters, it directly upgrades the first game's campaign experience. 

Cons
[list]
[*]Too short, not in a "not worth your money way", but in a "I need more way"
[*]Narrative structure too similar to the first Space Marine game: ohhh we're fighting xenos -> hehe chaos was lurking here
[*]Can't be replayed in a precise manner like in the first game, where each mission was separated by loadable checkpoints
[*][spoiler]♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Leandros[/spoiler]
[/list]

Pros:
[list]
[*]Decent - but small - boss roster 
[*]Characters with more personality and growth than in SM 1
[*]A good continuation to the first game story-wise, keeping in-line with what we learnt 
[*]Massive and Incredible spectacle both in gameplay, cinematics and overworld
[/list]

[h2]Operations (PVE Mode)[/h2]

Operations is a pve mode in which you participate in linear missions with random elements which are either directly related to the campaign or build on the situation after it. In Operations you can play six different classes, which are also avaliable in pvp, each having different functionalities, builds, weapons, and skill floors and ceilings. There are, at the time of writing, 7 different operations with 5 selectable difficulties (each recommended depending on your class level), with  new operations coming in the future as well as an already announced horde/waves mode (probably more similar to SM 1's coop pve).

Cons:
[list]
[*]Some classes feel extremely crutchy yet needed to play on higher difficulties 
[*]Some of the Operations are clearly not balanced for certain classes, so it might be difficult to beat them in matchmaking if the class compositions don't fit
[*]Although class customisation is a thing, balancing of perks and weapons is laking for some classes making build paths very limited towards anything thats not "meta"
[*]Reduced the power fantasy of the Assault class (Melee class with a jetpack to drop like a ballistic missile on enemies heads) compared to the Campaign and Pvp, removing its verticality and ability to shoot while in the air. 
[/list]

Pros:
[list]
[*]Expands on the boss roster and allows you to refight some of the campaigns bosses (Holds what is probably the best boss in the game)
[*]Builds on the narrative constructed in the campaign
[*]Replaying feels quite fresh due to random elements defining every node of a mission
[*]Allows for weapon and class customization to a decent degree
[*]All classes are, to different degrees, playable and enjoyable
[/list]

[h2]Eternal War (PVP Mode)[/h2]

SM 2's Eternal War drinks heavily from an older style of pvp shooter (such as Gears of War or the first Spacemarine title), having a much more slow, simple, yet cohesive gameplay. You're clearly limited by the rules set before you when it comes to movement, damage options and utility, and in no case does it feel like the more modern, strictly mechanical, faster than sound style of shooter. Not only that but it directly upgrades from the first game's pvp having double the classes, each fitting a playstyle and having it's own utility so that everyone can find something to enjoy. 

The mode as of time of writing has 3 gamemodes (TDM, Domination and Capture the Zone) and 3 completely symmetrical maps (with more coming in the future). I must point out that, for TDM, the maps being extremely symmetrical hurts the gameplay a bit, but to me it seems like a reasonable decision for the objective modes. This is a problem that the first game already had, and when your objective is not killing enemy players, but reaching an objective point with the same limitations as your opponents, it feels more boring yet fairer.

Cons:
[list]
[*]Lack of maps and map symmetry being quite extreme which might push some shooter players back
[*]Some weapons are unlocked extremely late in the progression making it grindy if you're just playing to try them out
[*]Fixed spawns might lead to occasions where you're spawn killed before the spawn switches sides
[*]No customisation for Chaos Marines other than colour
[*][spoiler]Freaking Carbine Sniper players, I hate you and you have a special spot in hell[/spoiler]
[/list]

Pros:
[list]
[*]Every class has a distinc personality and can fit into any team, having clearly more offensive and defensive classes, or ranged and melee classes
[*]Quite a bit of weapon options per class allowing for different playstyles with one same class
[*]Clean and tight finish that makes learning to play and winning very satisfying. 
[/list]

[h2]Closing Thoughts[/h2]

At some points I've compared this game to Gears of War, Sekiro and En Garde!, but another good comparison would be Remnant: From the Ashes, having a TPS in which you require precision both when shooting and defending, while facing bigger than life threats.

A spectacle of a Campaing that is satisfying both if you're lookin for challenging gameplay or simply to follow up on the first game's story. 
A pvp that is simple, old school and grounded with tons of aesthetic and loadout customisation but a bit lacking in maps. 
And lastly, and best of the bunch, a nice, replayable, fun coop mode that builds on the narrative and at higher difficulties can test your skill more than at the highest difficulty of the campaign, with customisable classes and weapons to make your own Space Marine loadout.
